c.tagline: Izmir's chic Aegean escape, famous for windsurfing beaches and a Genoese castle guarding the harbor

card: Widely accepted at hotels, restaurants, and boutiques; smaller beach kiosks may prefer cash.
rides: dolmuş minibuses to Alaçatı and Ilıca

taxi.fare: Roughly ₺30-50 flag fall plus metered per-km rate
taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; a fixed rate is common for the short trip to Alaçatı

walk: Central Çeşme's castle and harbor area are walkable, and Alaçatı's old town is similarly compact; getting between Çeşme, Alaçatı, and Ilıca requires a dolmuş, taxi, or rental car/scooter.

safety.safety: Very safe for solo travelers, including women; Çeşme and Alaçatı are upscale, well-established resort areas popular with Istanbul weekenders
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare; the town has a relaxed, low-crime resort atmosphere

hood_landmark.Alaçatı Old Town: Alaçatı's windmills and stone-house shopping streets

hood_desc: The historic harbor town centered on the 16th-century Genoese castle, with ferries, restaurants, and the Saturday market.
A chic restored Greek-heritage village of stone houses and windmills, now packed with boutique hotels, wine bars, and design shops.
The wide bay south of Alaçatı town, one of the world's top windsurfing and kitesurfing destinations thanks to steady summer winds.
A long sandy beach suburb popular for its shallow, calm swimming waters and beachfront hotels.
An upscale beach club district favored by Istanbul's weekend crowd for its stylish loungers and sunset bars.

water.note: Drink bottled water; tap water is not recommended here.

transit.sys: Dolmuş (shared minibus) network connecting Çeşme to Alaçatı and Ilıca
transit.map: Dolmuş depart from the main Çeşme otogar
transit.note: A rental scooter or car is popular for exploring the peninsula's beaches independently

transport.air: Izmir Adnan Menderes Airport (ADB), about 85 km away, has domestic and international flights
transport.bus: Regional coaches connect Çeşme to Izmir and other Aegean towns
transport.ferry: Seasonal ferries connect Çeşme to Chios, Greece
transport.car: Self-driving is popular for exploring the peninsula's beaches and Alaçatı independently

airport.name: Izmir Adnan Menderes Airport
airport.transport: Havaş shuttle buses and pre-booked hotel transfers; taxi transfer roughly $60-80

net.m: Good 4G/5G coverage in Çeşme and Alaçatı
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels and cafes
net.ap: A Turkcell or Vodafone tourist SIM or eSIM is recommended

tip.s: 10% is customary for tour guides and watersports instructors
tip.r: 10% is standard at restaurants where service isn't already included

food.name: Cesme kumru
food.desc: Sesame-crusted bread roll split and filled with local tulum cheese, tomato, sucuk and salami, then pressed hot on the griddle.

places.name: Tarihi Cesme Kumrucusu
places.note: Long-running kumru counter a short walk from the marina; the classic cheese-tomato-sucuk build.

places.name: Kumru stalls on Carsi Sokak
places.note: Cluster of griddle counters in the old bazaar; cheapest and busiest at lunchtime.

places.name: Alacati Pazar Yeri stalls
places.note: Market-square snack bars press kumru to order between browsing the produce stalls.

food.name: Ot yemekleri (Aegean wild herbs)
food.desc: Seasonal wild greens - sevketibostan, radika, deniz borulcesi, arapsaci - blanched and dressed with olive oil, lemon and garlic yoghurt.

places.name: Asma Yapragi
places.note: Alacati institution built around a daily table of olive-oil herb dishes; book ahead in summer.

places.name: Agrilia
places.note: Stone-walled Aegean kitchen known for foraged greens and its own olive oil.

places.name: Imren Lokantasi
places.note: Old-school tradesmen's canteen; point at the trays of herb dishes in the counter.

food.name: Grilled Aegean fish
food.desc: Whatever came off the boats that morning - sea bass, sea bream, barbun mullet or sardines - salted, grilled whole and served with rocket and lemon.

places.name: Ferdi Baba
places.note: Waterfront seafood institution in the fishing harbour; pick your fish from the ice.

places.name: Ata Balik
places.note: Reliable, unfussy fish house popular with locals rather than only holidaymakers.

places.name: Sota Alacati
places.note: Modern seafood kitchen praised in recent guides for grilled catch and raw plates.

food.name: Zeytinyagli meze table
food.desc: Cold olive-oil mezes - stuffed vine leaves, artichoke hearts, samphire, fava, black-eyed beans - laid out on a tray to choose from.

places.name: Cesme Deniz Restoran
places.note: Big meze tray brought to the table before the fish; harbour views.

places.name: Asma Yapragi
places.note: Meze counter is the whole point here; go early for the best spread.

places.name: Port Restaurant
places.note: Marina-side spot with a broad cold meze selection and grilled seafood.

food.name: Aegean village breakfast
food.desc: Sprawling kahvalti of local goat cheeses, tomato-egg menemen, olives, herb pastries, clotted cream and fig or mastic preserves.

places.name: Crete Kahvalti ve Sonrasi
places.note: Cretan-influenced breakfast house, one of the highest rated in town.

places.name: Kose Kahvalti Bahcesi
places.note: Garden breakfast tables in the old stone streets; big shared platters.

places.name: Alacati Pazar Yeri
places.note: Saturday market where the cheeses, olives and herb pastries actually come from.

food.name: Sakizli dondurma
food.desc: Chewy, stretchy ice cream thickened with Chios mastic gum, a Cesme peninsula speciality; also sold as karadut and cinnamon.

places.name: Rumeli Pastanesi
places.note: Making mastic ice cream and mastic sweets here since 1945; the local benchmark.

places.name: Rumeli Alacati
places.note: Branch of the same historic pastane on the main Alacati street.

places.name: Ice cream carts on Kemalpasa Caddesi
places.note: Evening carts along the promenade serve mastic ice cream in cones.

food.name: Sakizli limonata
food.desc: Cloudy lemonade infused with mastic gum, the peninsula's signature soft drink; also drunk as mastic-scented Turkish coffee.

places.name: Rumeli Pastanesi
places.note: Mastic lemonade and mastic Turkish coffee alongside the ice cream counter.

places.name: Cafes on Hacimemis Sokak
places.note: Shaded cafe street where mastic lemonade is the standard afternoon order.

places.name: Alacati Pazar Yeri stalls
places.note: Market vendors sell bottled mastic lemonade and mastic syrup to take home.

food.name: Raki
food.desc: Aniseed spirit clouded with water, drunk slowly through a fish-and-meze dinner rather than as an aperitif.

places.name: Ferdi Baba
places.note: Classic raki-and-fish table by the fishing boats.

places.name: Ata Balik
places.note: Meyhane-style evenings with meze, grilled fish and raki.

places.name: Arven Alacati
places.note: Winery restaurant for the alternative - around 200 Turkish and imported wines.

landmarks: Çeşme Castle (Çeşme Kalesi)
A commanding 16th-century Ottoman fortress above the marina, its ramparts and small archaeology museum overlooking the strait where the 1770 naval battle raged.
Alaçatı Old Town
A ravishing former Greek village of blue-shuttered stone houses, bougainvillea-draped lanes, and chic boutiques, now the Aegean's most fashionable weekend escape.
Alaçatı Windmills
A hilltop row of restored 19th-century stone windmills overlooking Alaçatı's rooftops, the region's signature sunset photograph and a nod to its grain-milling past.
Ilıca Beach
A kilometre of powdery white sand and shallow turquoise water, famous for warm thermal springs that bubble up directly through the seabed.
Aya Yorgi Bay
Çeşme's glamorous crescent of beach clubs and gin-clear water beneath St. George's hill, where Aegean summer nightlife meets daytime swimming perfection.
Ancient Erythrai (Ildırı)
The evocative hillside ruins of an Ionian League city near Ildırı village, its Hellenistic theatre gazing over olive groves to island-studded seas.
Çeşme Kervansaray (Ottoman Caravanserai)
A handsome stone caravanserai built in 1528 under Süleyman the Magnificent, its arcaded courtyard recalling the port's silk-and-spice trading heyday.
Çeşme Marina and İnkılap Street
The town's lively waterfront promenade and bazaar street, lined with yachts, seafood terraces, and shops selling the peninsula's famous mastic gum treats.
Church of Ayios Haralambos
A grand 19th-century Greek Orthodox basilica on the main street, now an exhibition hall whose weathered stone facade anchors Çeşme's old quarter.
Altınkum Beach (Golden Sand Beach)
A wild-feeling stretch of golden dunes and shockingly turquoise shallows south of town, beloved by locals for its laid-back beach shacks.

train.note: There is no railway on the Çeşme peninsula. The nearest stations are in İzmir, about an hour east, where the İZBAN suburban network and TCDD long-distance trains from Basmane connect to the rest of the country. Reach Çeşme by coach on the fast toll road or by car.

bus.note: No international coaches. Frequent buses run from Çeşme's otogar to İzmir Üçkuyular terminal in about an hour on the toll road, from where the national network fans out; some direct summer coaches also run to Istanbul and Ankara. Book through obilet (https://www.obilet.com/en/). Dolmuş minibuses serve Alaçatı and the surrounding beaches.

ferry.note: Çeşme is Turkey's busiest crossing to the Greek islands, with several daily sailings to Chios through the summer and a reduced winter timetable; Ertürk also carries vehicles. The harbour is right in the middle of town below the castle. Bring your passport, arrive about an hour ahead, and check Greek entry requirements - Chios has good onward connections to Piraeus and the other Aegean islands.

half.name: İzmir
half.blurb: Aegean port city with a Roman-era agora, a bayfront promenade, and a sprawling historic bazaar.

half.name: Sığacık & Teos
half.blurb: Walled fishing village next to the ruins of ancient Teos, once home to a major temple of Dionysus.

half.name: Foça
half.blurb: Fishing town on a small peninsula with Ottoman stone houses and offshore rock formations.
